We differentiate each component separately.

- For the $x$-component $x(t) = 10t^4,$ we have

$$
x'(t) = 40t^3,
$$

and therefore

$$
x'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 40\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 5.
$$

- For the $y$-component $y(t) = 6 \ln t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{6}{t},\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
y'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{6}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}=12.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) & =\left\langle {x}^{′}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right),\,{y}^{′}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨5,\,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We find the derivative of $f(t)$ by differentiating each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\left\langle \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡4t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6(t+5)^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(14-t)\right\rangle  \\  & =\left\langle \frac{4}{1+16{t}^{2}},12t+60,-1\right\rangle \end{aligned}
$$

We find ${f}^{′}(t)$ by differentiating each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t+1}) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{t})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{t+1} \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the derivative of  $f(t)=\begin{bmatrix}{t}^{2}+3t \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\end{bmatrix}$ at $t=1.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ by differentiating each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+3t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2t+3 \\ \frac{1}{t} \\ \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute ${f}^{′}(1)$ we substitute $t=1$ into the expression for ${f}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =\begin{bmatrix}2(1)+3 \\ \frac{1}{1} \\ \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi \cdot 1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2+3 \\ 1 \\ \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1 \\ -\pi \end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ by differentiating each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\left\langle \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7t)\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1,\,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute ${f}^{′}(\pi ),$ we substitute $t=\pi$ into the expression for ${f}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ),\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-1,\,7⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-4,\,7⟩\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Given that $\mathbf{f}(t)=\langle 2\cos t,\,3\sin t-t,\,t^2\rangle$, what is $\mathbf{f}\prime\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$?

$\mathbf{f}\prime\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=\langle$ {{field-1}} $,$ {{field-2}} $,$ {{field-3}} $\rangle$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First differentiate each component:

$$
\mathbf{f}\prime(t)=\left\langle -2\sin t,\,3\cos t-1,\,2t\right\rangle.
$$

Now substitute $t=\frac{\pi}{2}$ into the derivative, using $\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=1$ and $\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{f}\prime\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
&=\left\langle -2(1),\,3(0)-1,\,2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right\rangle \\
&=\langle -2,\,-1,\,\pi\rangle.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate each component separately, keeping the component order:

$$
\mathbf{f}\prime(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{d}}{{dt}}(t^3+2t) \\ \frac{{d}}{{dt}}(\cos t) \\ \frac{{d}}{{dt}}(e^t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3t^2+2 \\ -\sin t \\ e^t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The polynomial uses the power and sum rules, the derivative of $\cos t$ is $-\sin t$, and the derivative of $e^t$ is $e^t$.

Differentiate each scalar component, keeping the basis vectors fixed. The first component needs the product rule and the chain rule:

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(t\arctan(2t)\bigr)=\arctan(2t)+\frac{2t}{1+4t^2}.
$$

For the other two components,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}\ln(t+1)&=\frac{1}{t+1}, \\
\frac{d}{dt}(\cos t+t\sin t)&=-\sin t+\sin t+t\cos t=t\cos t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\mathbf{f}\prime(t)=\left(\arctan(2t)+\frac{2t}{1+4t^2}\right)\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{t+1}\mathbf{j}+t\cos t\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

Substitute $t=1$ only after differentiating:

$$
\mathbf{f}\prime(1)=\left(\arctan 2+\frac{2}{5}\right)\mathbf{i}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{j}+\cos 1\,\mathbf{k}.
$$

The angles are in radians; $\arctan 2$ and $\cos 1$ remain exact values.

Let $f_1$, $f_2$, and $f_3$ be the components in the given order. Differentiate each scalar component separately.

For component 1, use the product rule with inverse-tangent chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{1}'(t)&=\frac{d}{dt}\left(t \arctan{\left(3 t \right)}\right) \\ &=1\left(1\cdot \arctan{\left(3 t \right)}+t\cdot\frac{3}{1+(3 t)^2}\right) \\ &=\frac{3 t}{9 t^{2} + 1} + \arctan{\left(3 t \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

For component 2, use the sum and product rules; cancel opposite cosine terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{2}'(t)&=\frac{d}{dt}\left(3 t \cos{\left(t \right)} - 3 \sin{\left(t \right)}\right) \\ &=-3\left(\cos t-\cos t+t\sin t\right) \\ &=- 3 t \sin{\left(t \right)}
\end{aligned}
$$

For component 3, use the power and sum rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{3}'(t)&=\frac{d}{dt}\left(2 t^{2}\right) \\ &=4 t
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\mathbf{f}'(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3 t}{9 t^{2} + 1} + \arctan{\left(3 t \right)} \\ - 3 t \sin{\left(t \right)} \\ 4 t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Substitute $t=2$ into the derivative, after differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_{1}'(2)&=\frac{3 \left(2\right)}{9 \left(2\right)^{2} + 1} + \arctan{\left(3 \left(2\right) \right)} \\ &=\frac{6}{37} + \arctan{\left(6 \right)} \\ f_{2}'(2)&=- 3 \left(2\right) \sin{\left(\left(2\right) \right)} \\ &=- 6 \sin{\left(2 \right)} \\ f_{3}'(2)&=4 \left(2\right) \\ &=8
\end{aligned}
$$

Keeping the component order gives

$$
\mathbf{f}'(2)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{6}{37} + \arctan{\left(6 \right)} \\ - 6 \sin{\left(2 \right)} \\ 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$
